body: Marisetty and Subrahmanyam, 'Group Affiliation and the Performance of IPOs in the Indian Stock Market' (Journal of Financial Markets 13(1), 2010; ~110 citations): 2,713 Indian IPOs, 1990-2004, across three regulatory regimes. Indian underpricing was extreme in that era: average initial returns exceeded 100% in several years (as high as 689% in 1999). IPOs of private Indian business-group firms averaged about 140% initial returns and were MORE underpriced than stand-alone IPOs. The authors reject 'group certification' and attribute the extra underpricing to investor overreaction (it rises with oversubscription), while group affiliates had higher long-run survival because groups support affiliates to protect reputation. Deb and Marisetty, 'Information Content of IPO Grading' (Journal of Banking & Finance 34(9), 2010; ~120 S2 citations) studied SEBI's mandatory IPO grading (introduced 2007, made optional in 2014): higher-graded IPOs had lower underpricing and lower post-listing volatility, and grading raised retail demand for high-grade issues, which they read as reduced information asymmetry. Replicated: high Indian underpricing is confirmed in Ritter's international tables, and the post-2021 data show listing pops still common but long-run returns weak (insight:indian-ipo-long-run-returns). Use for us: listing-day gains are a lottery-ticket transfer from oversubscription and are not evidence of quality. Group brand does not certify an IPO. The long-run base rate favours waiting until 1-2 results after listing, then buying only on proof.

data.deb_marisetty: higher grade -> lower underpricing, more retail demand

title: Indian IPO underpricing: very high historically, highest for business-group IPOs (Marisetty-Subrahmanyam 2010, 2,713 IPOs); IPO grading cut underpricing (Deb-Marisetty 2010)
